about: Statistical model of the Oort Cloud (not a catalogue: no Oort Cloud body has ever been observed in place). Every point stands for millions of comets.

semiMajorAxis.source: Duncan, Quinn & Tremaine (1987, AJ 94, 1330): number density n(r) ~ r^-3.5 between 3,000 and 50,000 AU (dN/da ~ a^-1.5), about five times more comets inside 20,000 AU than outside. The rise below 2,000 AU and the cut-off beyond 50,000 AU are assumptions.
semiMajorAxis.note: dN/da is a continuous piecewise power law a^slope over the breaks. Points are drawn from the flatter 'samplingSlopes' law and carry the ratio of the two as a brightness weight, so the thin outer cloud still gets a third of the points.

perihelion.source: Detached orbits keep their perihelia beyond Neptune's reach (sednoids: 65-80 AU). Far out, the Galactic tide and passing stars randomise angular momentum, giving the thermal distribution f(e) = 2e (Heisler & Tremaine 1986). The eccentricity blends smoothly from detached to thermal across the transition range (a weighted mean of the two draws), which is an assumption.

orientation.source: Bodies start in the scattered disc near the ecliptic. The vertical Galactic tide precesses each orbit about the Galactic pole at a rate that grows steeply with semi-major axis, which twists the inner cloud into the spiral of Nesvorny et al. (2025, ApJ, arXiv:2502.11252: about 15,000 AU long, semi-major axes 1,000-10,000 AU); stellar encounters make the outer cloud isotropic. The isotropy range is an assumption.

tide.source: Local mass density of the Galactic disc 0.10 Msun/pc^3 (Holmberg & Flynn 2000, MNRAS 313, 209). Orbit-averaged vertical tide (Heisler & Tremaine 1986, Icarus 65, 13): node rate about the Galactic pole = -(nu^2 / 2n) cos(i_G) (1 + 1.5 e^2) / sqrt(1 - e^2), nu^2 = 4 pi G rho0, averaged over the argument of perihelion; e and i_G are held at their initial values. The rate uses the typical eccentricity at each semi-major axis (detached perihelion at the middle of its range inside, the thermal mean 2/3 outside, blended as the eccentricity is) rather than the orbit's own, with 15% (log-normal) scatter, because under the tide an orbit's eccentricity and inclination oscillate together, so its long-term rate is closer to the population's than its present eccentricity suggests; this is an assumption.

population.source: Boe et al. (2019, Icarus 333, 252): (1.5 +/- 1) x 10^12 Oort Cloud comets larger than 1 km, 1.3 +/- 0.9 Earth masses. Applied here to the outer cloud (a > 20,000 AU); the model then puts about five times as many closer in, as Duncan, Quinn & Tremaine (1987) found.

display.source: Visibility enhancement (not physical): the real cloud is far below any visible brightness. Point brightness shows how many comets a point stands for, not how much sunlight they reflect.
display.note: All artificial. A point of weight 1 at referenceDistanceAu gives referenceLux (times referenceCount / count and the brightness setting), falling as 1/d^2 so a haze's surface brightness does not depend on the viewing distance; d is bounded below by nearSpacings mean spacings (spacingFraction * a at referenceCount points, scaled by count^-1/3), so the nearest points never outshine the haze they belong to; capLux (about Sirius) is a safety net. contrast multiplies points beyond fromAu by (a / fromAu)^exponent, flattening the true r^-2.5 fall of the column density that no display can show. insideDim dims the whole cloud from 1 beyond toAu to min at fromAu (smooth in ln d), so the sky inside the dense cloud stays dark. Sprites are pointSizePx, growing to maxPointSizePx with half a spacing.
